newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore's new ethylene plant operates at 100-pct.
newsitem.headline: Singapore's new ethylene plant operates at 100-pct.

text.p: The Petrochemical Corporation of Singapore (PCS) is operating its new ethylene plant at full capacity even though two large downstream units have not started up yet, industry sources said on Wednesday.
They said PCS was able to do this because of strong ethylene demand in the regional spot market.
"The cracker is running at 100 percent and the extra ethylene is being exported," one source close to PCS said.
PCS is a 50:50 joint venture between Royal Dutch Shell and a consortium of Japanese companies led by Sumitomo Chemicals.

PCS started operating its new 515,000 tonnes per year (tpy) ethylene plant in late April and was initially expected to operate at between 70 and 80 percent of capacity due to the late startup of a 200,000-tpy polyethylene plant.

The polyethylene plant, which is 50-percent owned by Phillips Petroleum Singapore Chemicals, is expected to start up at the end of the third quarter, the source said. The remaining stake was held by Sumitomo Chemicals and Singapore's
The second downstream plant, Hoechst AG's 170,000-TPY vinyl acetate monomer (VAM) plant will only start up later this month or early next month.
PCS has an existing ethylene plant with a 450,000-tpy capacity.
Industry sources said ethylene demand remains strong despite the recent slide to spot prices by around $80 per tonne to just under $550 from a month ago.
As a result of PCS's unexpectedly high operating rate, spot naphtha supplies have tightened as surplus cargoes within the Singapore refining system are absorbed by the ethylene plant.
Apart from PCS, Thailand and South Korea were also in the market to pick up spot naphtha cargoes for use in new petrochemical plants.
Traders said the period of high demand coincided with a cut in supply due to shutdowns of crude units in Indonesia and a reduction in refining output in Singapore due to poor margins.
As a result, naphtha prices have risen by about $1.00 per barrel to $22.10 per barrel ($199 per tonne) within the past month.
Industry sources said all the derivative units that have already started up at the Singapore $3.4 billion petrochemical complex (US$2.36 billion) are operating at full capacity.
These include a 190,000-tpy polyethylene, 120,000-tpy polypropylene and a 450,000-tpy styrene monomer/propylene oxide plants.
